Field note / Dune systems

How a living dune holds its ground

Small changes can give windblown sand room to settle and grass room to take root.

A Tideland field note6 min read
The working questionHow can a public shore move without losing access?

The first thing you notice is the quiet. No engines, no straight lines—just sand rearranging itself under a steady wind.

A line of simple stakes crosses the dune. It is not a wall. It slows the wind long enough for beach grass to take root, while a marked path keeps the route open for people.

The work is easy to miss from the road: move a fence, close a shortcut, return a few plants to bare sand. Each choice gives the shoreline another option when rough weather arrives.

A living shore needs room to answer the weather.

The project treats the dune as shared infrastructure. It protects the path, the habitat, and the people who depend on the beach without asking the coast to become static.

By evening, the stakes sit low in the grass. The wind keeps moving. The dune keeps its shape by giving some of it away.
